lawyer:
Abdus Salam Khan, Advocate ----- For the Appellants. 
Miah Abdul Gofur, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
Abdul Awal and others ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Abdul Hamid and others ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 325 of 1963 affirming those of dated 31st July, 1963 passed by Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 31 of 1960. 

 2. The said suit was decreed by trial Court and on appeal the learned 3rd Court of Additional District Judge affirmed the decree of the trial Court. 

 3. Plaintiff respondent Abdul Hamid and others filed a Partition Suit being T.S. No. 31 of 1960 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for partition in respect of the land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 11 of Mouja Pakiabad PS Kapasia District Dhaka. In addition to the usual share inherited by plaintiff respondent 3.07 acres of land was claimed by way of partition on the basis of purchase as per registered kabala marked Ext. 1-C. 

 The land in suit was owned and possessed by 6 persons namely Abdul Aziz, Abdur Razzak, Dalema Bibi and Defendants 1-3 on equal shares on the strength of auction purchase in a certificate Case No. 271/29-30 and on confirmation of the certificate sale auction purchasers took delivery of possession through court and since then they remained in peaceful possession thereof. 

 5. Defendant No. 3 Ayes Ali alone contested the suit filing written statement. Defence case in short is, that suit property was owned by Adam who died leaving 6 sons namely Amir Ali, Jonah Ali, Nayab Ali, Kudrat Ali, Hossain Ali and Rustam Ali, and these 6 brothers made an amicable partition of the land in suit. Rustam Ali died leaving Lal Md. who lived with Amir Ali and CS record of right was prepared accordingly. Lal Md. died leaving his uncle and mother. Hossain Ali and Kudrat Ali sold their interest and left the place and thus three brothers namely Amir Ali, Jonab Ali and Nayab Ali possessed the entire suit property. The rent of their land in suit fell in arrears and the property was put to auction sale by the Bhowal Courts of Wards Estate. It was decided that the persons in possession of the land would pay arrear rent in proportion to quantum of land lying in their respective possession and accordingly Ares Ali and Dalema Bibi paid rent in respect of the land possessed by Amir Ali. Abdul Aziz and Mokkades paid the rent of land lying in possession of Jonab Ali. In 1353 BS all these persons decided to divide the land of the joma and accordingly they effected amicable partition of the land among themselves and as such further partition of the land in suit is not maintainable. 

 6. The learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka on consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary, passed the decree in preliminary form. Plaintiff respondent was allotted saham of one anna 5 gondas 2 krants 2/3rd danties covering 3.07 acres of land and other defendants were also allotted sahm in respect of the land lying in their possession. 

 7. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the decision of the trial Court appeal was preferred by the defendant appellant Ares Ali before the District Judge, Dhaka and the appeal on transfer was heard by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka who on reappraisal of the evidence concurred with the finding of the trial Court and passed decree affirming the decision of the trial Court. Defendant Ares All since dead being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 28.2.67 passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 31 of 1960 preferred this Second Appeal. 

 8. The grounds on which the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka has been attacked is that the learned Additional District Judge misread and misconstrued the judgment and decree Ext. C-2 and erred in holding the transaction was between plaintiff and his step-mother Azufa which was a private affair in which other co-sharers were not concerned. The learned Additional District Judge did not consider the registered document filed in lower appellate Court with a petition for admitting those-documents into evidence under Order 41 rule 27 of the CPC which would show that defendant got the land by purchase from other co-sharers and that the plaintiffs kabala Ext. 1-C was not legally proved and that it is hit under section 28 of Registration Act. Another ground taken in the memo of appeal is that the sale certificate was not acted upon as no delivery of possession was taken and that the purchasers in certificate case were in possession according to their respective previous possession but not in equal share. Further grounds taken in second appeal is' that in absence of writ of delivery of possession, sale certificate above-is not sufficient to prove auction purchase and as such story of auction purchase ought to have been disbelieved. 

 9. It is further urged by the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant that learned Additional District Judge did not consider the registered document filed in the Lower Appellate Court under Order 41 rule 27 CPC as additional evidence which would show that defendant got the land by purchase from other co-sharers. It is further urged that plaintiffs kabala -Ext. 1C is a void document under section 28 of tfie Registration Act inasmuch as insignificant portion of land has been included therein and this constitutes a fraud on registration law. 

 10. Both the Courts below on consideration of the materials on record concurrently held that certificate sale of the disputed holding took place and the sale was held in the year 1929-30. The sale certificate was produced before the trial Court and it was marked Ext. 1B and the validity of this document remains unchallenged. It may be mentioned here that at para 9 of the written statement certificate sale of the disputed property has been admitted. Since all the auction purchasers (six in number) were in possession of the auction purchased land and so no occasion arose for taking formal possession of the auction purchased land. But fact remains that plaintiffs title to the suit land accrued on the-basis of auction purchase in certificate sale held in the year 1929-30. 

 11. It has been found that both the courts below held that disputed holding was put to certificate sale in the year 1929 and the sale certificate Ext 1B is a positive proof of such certificate sale being held. It has already been referred that in the written statement the certificate, sale has been admitted. Therefore, the concurrent finding of the Courts below coupled with admission at para 9 of the written statement regarding auction sale proved beyond doubt that the holding in suit was put to certificate sale and the concurrent finding of courts below regarding certificate sale relates to the question of fact and High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with a finding of fact, however gross and inexcusable the error may seem to be, unless there is an error in the procedure provided by law which may possibly have produced an error or defect in the decision of the case on merit, If the lower appellate Court ignored some material evidence which might possibly have the effect of reversing the conclusion it would be an error or defect in the procedure of the same category as discarding evidence on the ground that it is inadmissible. An erroneous approach to the case will also be a defect in procedure if it substantially affects the merit of the case. But in the instant case no evidence was discarded on the ground of inadmissibility, neither any erroneous approach was made to the case. In view of this fact the concurrent finding of the Courts below coupled with admission in the written statement regarding sale of the disputed holding in a certificate proceeding undoubtedly relates, to the question of fact and it will stand undisturbed, even if such finding be held to be erroneous. 

 12. It is urged by the learned Advocate for the appellant that Additional District Judge did not consider registered document filed in the lower appellate Court under Order 41 rule 27 CPC as an additional evidence which would show that defendants got the land by purchase from other Co-sharers. From the order sheet of appellate Court record it appears that application supported by affidavit was filed before the appellate Court for adducing additional evidence but that application was not ultimately pursued. Order 41 rule 27 of the CPC speaks that Court is not bound under all circumstances mentioned in the rule to allow evidence as the parties are not entitled as of right to the admission of such evidence and the matter is entirely in the discretion of the Court. The approach of the appellate Court requires as mentioned under clause (b) of sub-rule 1 of the Order 48 it is only when the courts "requires it" i.e. finds it needful, that the additional evidence can be admitted. In other words, it has to be the requirement of the court itself for the purpose of giving a correct decision on proper appreciation of the evidence as it stands. The requirement must be genuine one and need for additional evidence must be felt by the Court itself after it has examined the evidence already on record and come to the conclusion that there is apparent and inherent lacuna or defect which hinders the due administration of justice. Additional evidence cannot be taken until the appellate Court has examined the evidence on record and has come to the conclusion that the evidence as it stands is inherently defective and unless additional evidence is allowed to be produced, the appellate Court cannot properly pronounce judgment. 

 But at the same time it is to be borne in mind that the admission of evidence should not be ordered to supplement the evidence of the party or to make up the weakness of his case and fill up the omissions. The discretion of the court should not be used in favour of the, plaintiff who was not diligent in getting the evidence filed although he could do so. The power under Order 41 rule 27 CPC is intended to be exercised when the court considers itself unable to pronounce judgment without further evidence. If the Court can deliver judgment the additional evidence should not be admitted. 

 13. The learned Advocate appearing for the defendant appellant submits that additional evidence ought to have been admitted as enjoined in clause (b) of rule 27 of Order 41 CPC to enable it pronounce judgment-or for any other substantial cause. "Apart from special causes mentioned in clauses (it) and (b) of Order 41 CPC the appellate Court has the power to accept additional evidence "for any other substantial cause," such as doing complete justice between the parties. The power to allow additional evidence should be exercised occasionally and sparingly and only in exceptional case and new evidence to be admissible should have a direct and important bearing on the main issue in the case. In absence of satisfactory reason for non production of the evidence in trial Court additional evidence should not be admitted in appeal because a party guilty of negligence in the lower court is not entitled to the indulgence of being allowed to give further evidence under this Rule. Provisions of this Rule are not intended to allow a litigant who has been unsuccessful in the lower court to patch up the weak part of a case and fill up omission In the Court of appeal. In the Instant case certain documents were filed before the appellate Court for its admission into evidence but ultimately that application was not pursued by the defendant appellant. Moreover, this operates as check against easy reception of evidence at a late stage of litigation. 

 14. Thus it is found that the requirement of the court itself is for the purpose of giving correct decision. on proper appreciation of the evidence as it stands but the appellate Court did not consider the additional evidence to enable him to pronounce the judgment Therefore, for the reason stated above the objection raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the Additional District Judges did not consider the registered document under Order 41 rule 27 does not merit consideration and as such it is overruled inasmuch as no satisfactory reason has been assigned why those documents were not produced at the trial Court during trial. 

 16. Thus having considered the, entire evidence on record and the legal aspects of the matter I am led to the conclusion that the Six persons whose names appear in the sale certificate Ext. 1B are the real owners of the disputed property in equal share and that decree passed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court in Title Appeal No. 325 of 1963 is based on proper appreciation of evidence and as such it does not call for any interference.
